message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) diverged very early in mammalian evolution.  
Their most recent common ancestor was a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived about 70–80 million years ago, during the late Cretaceous. That ancestor was the base of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, from which one branch led eventually to the order *Carnivora* (the lion’s lineage) and another branch led to the order *Perissodactyla* (the zebra’s lineage). In other words, the last common ancestor of a lion and a zebra was a tiny, generalized mammal that gave rise to the entire Laurasiatherian radiation.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. This is a biology question. We need to answer. There's no tool needed. Just provide an answer. Probably mention that lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) share a common ancestor within the order Carnivora? Wait, lions are mammals, specifically within the family Felidae, subfamily Pantherinae. Zebras are equids, family Equidae. Both belong to class Mammalia, phylum Chordata. Their most recent common ancestor would be at the level of the mammalian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species. That would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae. That would be somewhere in the order of placental mammals. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But if we want more specific: The last common ancestor of the two species would be the ancestor of the clade that includes both families, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually, Felidae and Equidae are part of the superorder Laurasiatheria. Within Laurasiatheria, the last common ancestor might be the ancestor of the group that includes Perissodactyla (horses, rhinos, tapirs) and Cetartiodactyla (even-toed ungulates). But lions are carnivores, so they are in the clade Carnivora. So the last common ancestor of Felidae and Equidae would be the ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That is the ancestor of the clade called Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the ancestor of Laurasiatheria. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species is the ancestor of the clade that includes both families, which is the ancestor of the clade that includes all placental mammals. But we can say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived around 70 million years ago, during the late Cretaceous period. That ancestor gave rise to the lineages leading to the modern orders Carnivora (lion lineage) and Perissodactyla (zebra lineage). So the answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, likely insectivore-like mammal from the late Cretaceous, the ancestor of the Laurasiatheria clade.
